    Moshe Vaknin
    3w

    An OM is a marketing document. That is not an accusation. It is the job. And nothing in it has to be false for all of it to point one way. One deal we looked at this summer, a 2000 build in a good submarket: • Expenses underwritten at 38% of income. The T-12 in the same folder said 54%. • A loss to lease in the model, while the OM's own footnote and the T-12 both showed a gain to lease. • The entire rent upside thesis built on the comp's asking rents. On effective rents the gap was six points smaller, and the subject was already giving 10% concessions. • Net of all that, a pro forma NOI 70% above trailing. Every one of those choices is defensible on its own. Together they point in exactly one direction. Here is the part that costs money. None of it was hidden. The rent roll and the T-12 were in that folder from day one. But the OM is the only file in there a person can actually read. Forty pages, built to be read, sitting next to a 2,200 row rent roll and a 200 row income statement. So the OM decides. Not because anyone trusts it, but because reconciling it by hand is a week of your best analyst, per deal. You either screen on the marketing and get pulled deep into a deal that dies at IC, or you verify properly and screen half as many. Either way, the OM just chose what your team spent the quarter on. It does not have to work that way. Hand over the whole folder at once, ask one question, and get the OM's numbers standing next to the rent roll's and the T-12's, line by line, while you are still deciding whether to open the deal at all. The reconciliation stops being week two of the process and becomes the first ten minutes of it. Then the screen is a decision you made, not one the OM made for you. How many deals did your team underwrite last year, and how many did you buy? The gap between those two numbers is the real budget. #MultifamilyInvesting #RealEstateAcquisitions #CRE #RealEstateCapital lizo.ai

    "Turn a needle in a haystack into a needle in a pile of needles."

    Moshe Vaknin
    3w

    "I have $50M sitting in the bank. It's been a year and I still haven't found a deal." A multifamily owner told me this last week. My first thought was that it's expensive. $50M in cash for a year isn't capital waiting to be deployed. It's capital not earning what it was raised to earn, and the wait compounds. But the part that stayed with me was why. He isn't sitting out because there are no deals. He looked at maybe fifty this year. His markets traded thousands. He didn't reject the rest. He never saw them. His team can give a real look to a few teasers a week, so the buy box only ever gets applied to whatever happened to land on top of the pile. The deal worth $50M could have come in on a Tuesday in March and nobody would know. His words, not mine: he wants to turn a needle in a haystack into a needle in a pile of needles. That's a capacity problem wearing a market problem's clothes. The deals are there. The only question is how many of them ever get looked at. #MultifamilyInvesting #RealEstateAcquisitions #CRE #RealEstateCapital lizo.ai

    The whole pile instead of the top of it

    Moshe Vaknin
    1mo

    Every acquisition leader I talk to agrees the market moves fast. Their team isn't. Not for lack of skill. It's the tools. Manual sheets, copy paste between systems, every deal email opened and screened by hand. Do the arithmetic on that. Five to ten deal blasts land in the inbox every day. A proper first pass costs three to four hours. One analyst clears two a day, on a good day. So the rest of the pile gets triaged on instinct. Sender, market, a number in the subject line. Twenty years of pattern recognition applied in four seconds, to markets that no longer exist. The deal you needed was in that pile. It didn't get four hours. It got four seconds. That's the cost nobody underwrites. Not the deals you analyzed and passed on. The ones that were never opened. We built lizo.ai so that arithmetic stops mattering. First-pass underwriting in minutes instead of hours, against your buy box, on every deal that lands rather than the two you had time for. Same team, same instincts, the whole pile instead of the top of it. The deals worth your capital are rare, and they go to whoever reaches them first. lizo.ai #MultifamilyInvesting #RealEstateAcquisitions #CRE

    If you're sitting on capital and waiting for the market to tell you it's safe, message us.

    Moshe Vaknin
    1mo

    A lot of investors I talk to right now are waiting. Rates are high, debt is expensive, and values are under pressure. So the instinct is to sit tight until the market feels safer. But hard markets don't eliminate opportunity. They create it, through distress, refinancing pressure, and owners who need to sell. And that window won't stay open forever. There are two ways to lose in this market: miss the deal that could have driven your returns, or put your capital behind the wrong one. Most investors are so focused on avoiding the second that they risk walking straight into the first. lizo surfaces the deals worth your capital and gives you a clear pursue-or-pass decision. Not another dashboard to interpret. Not another pile of data. A decision. And because every opportunity gets evaluated, the best deal doesn't stay buried just because your team ran out of time. Your capital goes where the return potential is strongest, before someone else gets there first. If you're sitting on capital and waiting for the market to tell you it's safe, message me. I'll show you what we're finding right now. #Multifamily #CRE #RealEstateCapital #CREDebt

    A decision is only as good as what it's built on. Last week, an investor showed me an analysis he had run on a potential acquisition using one of the general AI chat tools. It looked sharp - well-argued, well-sourced, the kind of analysis you feel you can act on. He was close to moving on the deal. Then we looked at the data behind it: advertised rents from one source, a rent-growth figure from another, and a comps set built around properties that weren't truly comparable. The analysis was built on publicly available information that simply didn't line up. So I suggested we run the same asset through lizo. It came back with the opposite call: pass. The rents the AI chat relied on were asking rents, while effective rents were much lower. Its rent-growth figure pointed up, while the submarket was softening. And its comp set compared the asset with properties from a different class - meaning the pricing and operating assumptions were not truly comparable. Based on the underlying data, the deal didn't work. The problem isn't the AI itself. A general AI chat can only reason over the information it can access. The harder part is knowing which data is actually relevant, how different sources should be reconciled, and which assumptions belong together in the same investment picture. It can sound certain. But certainty is a writing style, not a measure of data quality. Same asset, same afternoon. The AI gave him a report. lizo gave him a decision he could act on. If you're screening deals this quarter, the question worth asking isn't just what the analysis concluded. It's what the decision was built on. See how lizo turns the data into a pursue-or-pass decision: https://www.lizo.ai/decide #Multifamily #CRE #Acquisitions #RealEstateAI #RealEstate
